doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Back to Chicago and the road to jail and illness
title: Borrowed basses, the local 208 delegate and the folded concerts
summary: Ware gets a new fiddle through friends, the concert plan founders on union trouble, and he is stuck at DeFore's house.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x:
all around the South Side and the North Side of Chicago.
So I'm making contact with all those folks, you know, everybody that hadn't seen me, since I made my big debut in New York; however, I didn't have a fiddle, naturally. I got rid of the fiddle that I did have, and an old army buddy of mine, Karl Ervin -- Smitty we used to call him in the service; a young fellow, he needed money then, and called on him and he wanted to know what was happening, and he said; "Got a fiddle? I'll buy you one." (inaudible) and at the time, I found out that Malachi who I knew at the time, was working in with we were going at it as a trio, and Andrew Hill, and he had a fiddle that he wanted to sell, so Karl bought that for me, so I had myself another fiddle to play these engagements.

Now, I don't realize that De Fore Duflores (phonetic) was having problems with the black local there; local 208; that was before they merged, and they wanted him to put up so much money and he wouldn't do it. And when it was time to do a concert, what you call -- one of the delegates was trying to tell him, you can't play, you ain't gonna play and telling us not to play, and hell, I needed the money; I came all the way from New York to play this concert.

Anyway, we played. It wasn't a good turnout but we got paid; I got paid, you know, Griffin got paid, Phil Thomas got paid and Jody Jerry got paid and, Henry Richard Brown was the walking delegate; walking around with his [twisted] leg, you know, and that knocked the concerts out, because he

Rollins; couldn't contact Sonny Robinson; he was supposed to come in, Coltrane maybe about a week later, or two weeks later, and Cole Train was supposed to come in two or three weeks following that; you know, just as singles, to use our rhythm section. So, that folded.

So I'm stuck in Chicago now, but I'm happy to be home. I got a chance to relax some; I'm staying at his house, and I was kind of babysitting, because they had a little girl there, and when Don and his wife would cut out, I'd sit with the baby and have a few friends over, you know, and that was it. And I wanted to get around and see somebody, and started visiting some of the old guys in the neighborhood; went over to see there was a club called McKee's Chris Anderson and Leo, and (unintelligible) and they'd bring Sutherland in different bands, and as well, the Southern Hotel. They was bringing in groups like Miles and Cannonball and Ornette this was in the early sixties.
